claims.text: A deep-neural-network-potential molecular-dynamics framework can precisely predict melting behavior in high-entropy alloy carbonitrides.
The framework can determine fusion enthalpy and fusion entropy accurately.
The framework can determine the volume change at melting accurately.
The framework can determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties accurately.
(TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1-x is an example of the targeted high-entropy carbonitride system.
Deep-neural-network-potential simulations can describe both the solid and liquid structures of (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1-x.
Heating and cooling simulations can be used to determine the melting temperature and associated atomistic structural changes.
The neural-network potential is calibrated to reproduce DFT-level atomic interactions.
A temperature interval of approximately 3000–4000 K encompasses the melting transition of the targeted carbonitrides.
Constant-pressure simulation conditions mimic experimental melting environments.
Bonding in the carbonitrides involves strong hybridization between metal d-electrons and carbon or nitrogen s,p-electrons.
C≡N triple-bond contributions participate in the bonding rationale.
Bond hybridization and liquid-state structural or entropic changes cause a nonlinear enhancement of melting temperature as nitrogen is added.
Resolving energetic differences and structural rearrangements at melting quantifies latent heat and thereby enables determination of enthalpic, entropic, and volumetric changes.
Melting temperatures can be predicted with an error margin of ±30 K.
Melting temperature increases nonlinearly with increasing nitrogen content.
Traditional DFT, Lindemann-criterion, and Born-criterion methods do not directly simulate homogeneous melt nucleation and detailed liquid-state properties.

The approach is applicable to other high-entropy alloy systems with similar metal–nonmetal orbital hybridization but may not transfer to fundamentally different bonding environments or transition mechanisms.
Predictive accuracy depends critically on the quality and representativeness of the DFT training data, and extrapolation beyond trained compositions or temperatures may reduce reliability.
Experimental melting-temperature measurement is resource-intensive, while an efficient computational predictor could support screening of refractory-material databases.
